beats.text: Jallianwala Bagh. 13 April 1919.
A garden in Amritsar. A banned meeting. A general who decided to teach a city a lesson.
The Rowlatt Act. March 1919. It allowed detention without trial. Across Punjab, protests began.
The route: the order, the garden, the firing, the inquiry, and the argument that never ended.
Baisakhi. 13 April 1919. Thousands gathered in the Bagh for the festival and to protest the arrest of two local leaders.
The Bagh was about two hundred yards square. Its walls were ten feet high. It had five narrow entrances.
The meeting began at half past five. Dyer arrived an hour later with about fifty soldiers and blocked the main exit.
A crowd is not a target. The distinction is the whole argument.
Without a warning to disperse, Dyer ordered his troops to fire into the crowd.
The firing lasted about ten minutes. Dyer later reported that his party fired 1,650 rounds.
The official inquiry counted 379 dead and more than 1,200 wounded. Other estimates were higher.
Some died at the narrow gates. Some died in the well. The wounded lay where they fell under curfew.
The Hunter Commission criticised Dyer. It did not prosecute him.
He was relieved of his command and barred from employment in India. He was never tried for murder.
An inquiry that names a failure without punishing it teaches the next officer what the state will tolerate.
Britain has never formally apologised. In 2019 it expressed deep regret.
The massacre helped turn the Congress toward mass non-cooperation in 1920 and 1921.
The Empire called it an incident. India called it a massacre. The words were part of the fight.
Official inquiry: 379 dead. More than 1,200 wounded. One garden. One order.
The Raj survived the inquiry. It did not survive the loss of trust.
The question is not whether the Empire could kill. It is what a country does with the memory.
